Electromagnetic charge is the winding number of this phase around the \mathrm{U}(1) fiber of the Hopf map \mathrm{SU}(2) \to \mathbb{CP}^1.
  3. The symplectic pairing on the color tube coordinates. The T-duality involution \iota \colon (X, z) \mapsto (z, X) on the symmetric cubic F(X, z) = F(z, X) exchanges color and spacetime degrees of freedom. The symplectic form \omega = dX \wedge dz is invariant under \iota. The Coulomb interaction is the component of the crossing energy that transforms as a (1,1)-form under the complex structure.

  • Charge quantisation. Q is an eigenvalue of an involution, hence discrete (\pm 1 for leptons, \pm 1/3, \pm 2/3 for quarks in the Borromean decomposition).

prop:weak-vertex-left-projector:
Proposition The weak vertex insertion is proportional to the left projector. Let \sigma be a generator of H_n(q), so that \sigma^2 = h\,\sigma + 1 with h = q - q^{-1}, and assume q \neq 0 and [2]_q = q + q^{-1} \neq 0. The generator has two eigenlines: the line on which it acts by q, with projector P_+ = (\sigma + q^{-1})/[2]_q, and the line on which it acts by -q^{-1}, with projector P_- = (q - \sigma)/[2]_q.

The left line P_L is the eigenline on which \sigma acts with an eigenvalue of modulus greater than 1, and the right line P_R = 1 - P_L is the other one. For |q| > 1 this gives P_L = P_+. The weak vertex W is the element that acts as \sigma^{-1} on the left line and as \sigma on the right line:

W \;=\; \sigma^{-1} P_L + \sigma\, P_R .

The difference between the weak vertex and the free crossing is a multiple of the left projector:

W - \sigma \;=\; -(q - q^{-1})\, P_L .

This holds for |q| > 1 and for |q| \leq 1. Three consequences follow.

  1. The difference W - \sigma annihilates the right line, and it acts on the left line by the scalar -(q - q^{-1}). It vanishes exactly when q - q^{-1} = 0.
  2. An element a + b\,\sigma annihilates the right line if and only if it is a scalar multiple of P_L. Within the algebra generated by one crossing, "the right line does not couple" and "proportional to P_L" are the same statement.
  3. Let t be the eigenvalue of \sigma of modulus greater than 1, whichever of q and -q^{-1} that is, and weight the positive crossing by it. Then the weighted crossing difference is
t\,\sigma - t^{-1}\sigma^{-1} \;=\; (t - t^{-1})(t + t^{-1})\, P_L .

So the choice of which crossing carries the weight, left open in the force-carrier identification, is the same choice as the left line.

Scope at the level of a knot. The statement is about one crossing. It does not extend to the trace of the weak knot T_{3,5}, the closure of (\sigma_1\sigma_2)^5 in H_3(q). Under the Markov trace \mathrm{tr}_M at z = q^3/(q^2+1), the part of that trace on the right line of \sigma_1 is

\mathrm{tr}_M\bigl((\sigma_1\sigma_2)^5\, P_R\bigr) \;=\; -\frac{q^2}{(q^2+1)^3} \;\neq\; 0 .

At the proton-anchored q_0 this is -9.33\,\% of \mathrm{tr}_M\bigl((\sigma_1\sigma_2)^5\bigr). All of it comes from the two-dimensional block of H_3(q), since y_{(1^3)} = 0 at z = q^3/(q^2+1). For the torus words (\sigma_1\sigma_2)^N the right-line part repeats with period 3 in N and is never zero.

This holds for every trace with y_{(2,1)} \neq 0, not only at z = q^3/(q^2+1). Write a trace on H_3(q) as \tau = y_{(3)}\chi_{(3)} + y_{(2,1)}\chi_{(2,1)} + y_{(1^3)}\chi_{(1^3)}. Assume |q| > 1, so that P_R = P_-, and [3]_q \neq 0. Then \tau(x P_R) = 0 for every x if and only if y_{(2,1)} = y_{(1^3)} = 0. With \tau(1) = 1, such a trace is the augmentation \sigma_i \mapsto q; it already suffices that \tau vanish on P_R and on \sigma_2 P_R. Since y_{(2,1)} = q^2/(q^2+1)^2 \neq 0 at z = q^3/(q^2+1), no word-level one-sidedness holds.

Where the weak vertex comes from. The definition of W rests on two inputs that are chosen, not derived.

  1. The one-sided requirement. W is required to act as \sigma^{-1} on one eigenline of \sigma and as \sigma on the other. This is an ansatz.
  2. The side. The eigenline on which W acts as \sigma^{-1} is the left line, by the definition of P_L above.

Given the two inputs, W is unique: an element x with x P_+ = a P_+ and x P_- = b P_- equals a P_+ + b P_-. With J = P_+ - P_- and |q| > 1, the two one-sided elements are

\sigma^{-1} P_+ + \sigma P_- \;=\; q^{-1} J, \qquad \sigma P_+ + \sigma^{-1} P_- \;=\; q\, J .

So W = q^{-1}J, and the element with the opposite side, qJ, differs from it only by the scalar q^2. The Proposition above follows from the inputs and is, in this sense, close to a restatement of them.

What this does not say. It does not identify W with the physical weak coupling.

Proof Proof of the weak vertex insertion identity. Since P_L + P_R = 1, every element x satisfies x = x P_L + x P_R. By definition W P_L = \sigma^{-1} P_L and W P_R = \sigma P_R. Hence

If x P_R = 0, then x = x P_L = (a + b\mu)\, P_L, where \mu is the eigenvalue of \sigma on the left line. The converse is P_L P_R = 0.
